questions.stem_markdown: At a routine adolescent clinic review in Sydney, the registrar asks to spend part of a 15-year-old’s consultation alone with the young person, even though the parent is supportive and wants to stay. Which explanation best matches the interview approach described in the notes?

options.text: This is mainly done only when abuse or another immediate safety concern is already suspected
It supports engagement and allows confidential discussion of psychosocial issues that are part of adolescent assessment
It is mainly used to show that parents should no longer contribute to the history
It is done only to determine whether the young person can independently consent to every treatment
It is only appropriate if alcohol or drug use has already been disclosed

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes place **HEEADSS assessment** within adolescent care and separately state that comprehensive adolescent assessment should include **engagement and discussion of confidentiality**. Asking to spend part of the review with the young person alone is therefore best explained as supporting confidential psychosocial assessment and rapport, rather than excluding the parent or serving only as a consent test.

why_others_wrong.A: The note-based approach frames adolescent psychosocial assessment as broader than situations where abuse or immediate safety concerns are already suspected.
why_others_wrong.C: The notes discuss supporting parents in the health system, so time alone with the young person is not presented as removing parents from care entirely.
why_others_wrong.D: The consent section addresses mature minor and treatment consent separately; it does not make one-on-one interview time merely a test of independent consent for every decision.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes link confidentiality to comprehensive adolescent assessment and do not restrict this approach only to consultations where substance use has already been disclosed.

key_takeaways: Adolescent assessment includes structured psychosocial screening such as HEEADSS.
The notes explicitly pair adolescent engagement with discussion of confidentiality.
Seeing a young person alone for part of a review is different from excluding parents or performing only a consent assessment.
